title: Back Pain After Drinking: Muscle, Kidney, or Pancreas?
excerpt: Why your back hurts after drinking, how to tell muscle pain from kidney or pancreas pain, what helps at home, and the warning signs that mean you should see a doctor.
metaDescription: Why does your back hurt after drinking? How to tell muscle aches from kidney or pancreas pain, what helps, and the signs that mean you should see a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** most back pain after a night of drinking comes from your muscles, not your organs. Dehydration, a few hours asleep in an awkward position on a couch or a bad mattress, dancing or standing in heels all night, and the general inflammation of a hangover can all leave your back stiff and sore the next day. That kind of ache usually feels dull and spread out, gets worse when you move a certain way, and fades within a day or two with water, food, rest, and gentle movement.

A smaller share of back pain after drinking comes from organs that sit near your back: the **kidneys** (pain in the flank, just under the ribs on one or both sides), and the **pancreas** (deep pain in the upper belly that bores straight through to the middle of the back). Those are the ones worth knowing about, because pancreatitis and kidney problems can be serious. This guide walks through how to tell the difference, what you can do at home, and the specific signs that mean you should see a doctor instead of waiting it out.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and common patterns. It can't diagnose your pain. **Get medical care the same day if** you have severe pain in your upper belly that spreads to your back, especially with vomiting; pain in your side or flank with fever, chills, or burning when you pee; blood in your urine; pain so strong you can't get comfortable in any position; or back pain with numbness, weakness in your legs, or trouble controlling your bladder or bowels. **Call 911 or go to the emergency room** for sudden, severe back or chest pain, fainting, confusion, or vomiting blood. If you drink heavily every day and feel shaky, sweaty, or very anxious when you stop, tell a doctor, because stopping suddenly can be risky and medical help makes it safer.

## Quick Guide: Where Does It Hurt?

The location and feel of the pain is the best clue you have. This table is a starting point, not a diagnosis.

| Where it hurts | What it feels like | Most likely cause | How urgent |
|---|---|---|---|
| Lower back, across both sides, in the muscles | Dull, stiff, achy; worse when you bend or twist; better when you change position | Muscle strain, sleeping position, dehydration, general hangover aches | Usually fine to treat at home |
| Flank (side of the back, under the ribs), one or both sides | Deeper ache, not much affected by moving; may come with needing to pee a lot | Dehydration and kidney strain, sometimes a kidney stone or infection | See a doctor if it's severe, one-sided and sharp, or comes with fever, chills, or blood in urine |
| Upper middle back, with pain in the upper belly | Steady, boring pain that goes straight through to the back; worse lying flat, may ease leaning forward; nausea and vomiting | Possible pancreatitis | Get medical care the same day |
| Right upper back or under the right shoulder blade, with right upper belly pain | Cramping or steady pain, often after a big fatty meal | Possible gallbladder problem | See a doctor, urgently if you have fever or yellow skin |
| Pain that started with a fall, a twist, or lifting | Sharp, localized, may shoot down a leg | Injury to muscle, disc, or spine | See a doctor if it's severe or there's numbness or weakness |

## Why Your Back Hurts After Drinking: The Muscle Causes

Let's start with the common, mostly harmless reasons. If your pain fits these, it's very likely muscular.

### Dehydration and electrolyte loss

Alcohol suppresses a hormone called vasopressin (also known as antidiuretic hormone), which normally tells your kidneys to hold onto water. With less of it around, you pee more than you drink. You lose water along with minerals like sodium, potassium, and magnesium, which your muscles need to contract and relax properly.

Muscles that are short on water and electrolytes are more prone to tightness and cramping. The big muscles that run along your spine work all day to keep you upright, so they're one of the first places that tightness shows up. That's why a dehydrated back often feels stiff and achy rather than sharply painful.

The fix is simple and boring: water, plus some electrolytes. Our guide to [electrolytes and alcohol](/never-hungover/electrolytes-and-alcohol) covers which minerals matter and the easiest ways to replace them.

### Sleeping in a bad position

This is probably the single most common cause, and it's easy to overlook. Alcohol makes you fall asleep fast and sleep heavily in the first part of the night. When you're sober, you shift position many times a night without noticing, partly because your body registers discomfort. After several drinks, that feedback is dulled. You can spend hours twisted on a couch, curled in a car seat, or flat on your stomach with your neck turned, and your back pays for it in the morning.

If you woke up somewhere other than your own bed, or in a position you don't normally sleep in, that's a strong hint.

### A long night on your feet

Standing at a bar or a party for hours, dancing, walking between venues, or wearing heels or unsupportive shoes all load your lower back. Alcohol also blunts the aches that would normally tell you to sit down. The bill arrives the next morning.

### Hangover inflammation

A hangover isn't just dehydration. Research on hangovers has found that heavy drinking is followed by changes in inflammatory signaling molecules (cytokines) in the body, and many researchers think this immune response explains part of why a hangover feels like a mild flu: body aches, tiredness, and feeling run down. General muscle aches, including in the back, fit that picture. Our [hangover symptoms guide](/never-hungover/hangover-symptoms) explains the full set of symptoms and what drives each one.

### Minor injuries you didn't notice

A stumble on the stairs, a twisted step off a curb, or carrying a friend to a cab can strain a muscle without registering much at the time, because alcohol dulls pain. If one specific spot is sore and tender to press, and it hurts more with certain movements, think back over the night.

### How muscle pain feels

Muscle-related back pain usually has these features:

- It's on both sides or across the lower back, in the thick muscles beside the spine.
- It's stiff and achy rather than sharp and stabbing.
- It changes when you move, bend, twist, or press on it.
- It improves over the day as you rehydrate, eat, and move around.
- You feel otherwise like a normal hangover, with no fever and no vomiting that won't stop.

## Kidney Pain After Drinking

People often search "kidney pain after drinking" when their back hurts, and it's a fair question. The kidneys sit high in the back, on either side of the spine, tucked just under the lower ribs. Kidney pain is usually felt in the **flank**: the area on your side between the bottom of your ribs and the top of your hip, toward the back. It's higher and more to the side than typical lower-back muscle pain.

### Why drinking can make your kidneys ache

- **Dehydration.** Because alcohol makes you pee more, a night of drinking can leave you dehydrated. Some people notice a dull ache in the kidney area that fades once they rehydrate. It's usually not a sign of damage on its own, but it's a clear signal to drink water.
- **Kidney stones.** Dehydration concentrates your urine, which is one of the conditions that favors kidney stones. Alcohol doesn't directly cause stones, but heavy drinking plus not much water can play a part. Beer is also relatively high in purines, which raise uric acid, a factor in one type of stone. A stone moving through the tube from the kidney to the bladder causes some of the worst pain people describe: sharp, coming in waves, often on one side, sometimes moving toward the groin, often with nausea.
- **Urinary or kidney infections.** Alcohol doesn't cause infections, but an existing bladder infection can travel up to the kidneys, and a night of drinking can mask early symptoms. A kidney infection usually comes with fever, chills, burning when you pee, cloudy or bad-smelling urine, and pain in the flank.
- **A narrowing where the kidney drains (rare).** Some people have a partial blockage where the kidney meets the tube that drains it, called a ureteropelvic junction (UPJ) obstruction. Drinking a large volume of fluid, beer especially, makes the kidney fill faster than it can drain, and that stretching causes flank pain. If you get the same one-sided flank pain every time you drink a lot of beer, mention it to a doctor. It shows up on imaging.

### How kidney pain feels

- Higher and more to the side than muscle pain, just below the ribs.
- Deep, and not much affected by moving or stretching.
- Often on one side, though dehydration can cause a mild ache on both.
- Can come with changes in your urine: very dark, cloudy, painful to pass, or tinged with blood.

### Does drinking damage your kidneys?

For an occasional social drinker, a night out is unlikely to harm healthy kidneys. Regular heavy drinking is a different story. It raises blood pressure over time, which is one of the main drivers of chronic kidney disease, and it's tied to liver disease, which can affect kidney function too. Binge drinking can also, rarely, cause a sudden drop in kidney function in people who become severely dehydrated. We cover the longer-term picture in our article on [alcohol and kidney health](/never-hungover/alcohol-kidney-disease-renal-function-impact-2025).

## Upper Back Pain After Drinking: The Pancreatitis Warning

This is the section to read carefully. **Pancreatitis** means inflammation of the pancreas, the organ behind your stomach that makes digestive enzymes and insulin. Heavy drinking and gallstones are the two most common causes of acute pancreatitis. It can follow a single heavy binge, but it's much more common in people who drink heavily over months or years.

The pancreas lies deep in the upper abdomen, right in front of the spine. When it's inflamed, the pain is felt in the upper belly and very often **spreads straight through to the middle of the back**. That's why "upper back pain after drinking" deserves attention when it comes with stomach symptoms.

### Signs that point toward pancreatitis

- Severe, steady pain in the upper middle belly (just below the breastbone), often moving through to the back
- Pain that's worse after eating or when lying flat on your back, and may ease a little when you sit up and lean forward
- Nausea and repeated vomiting
- A swollen, tender belly
- Fever or a fast heartbeat
- Feeling very unwell, far worse than a normal hangover

**If this sounds like you, get medical care the same day.** Acute pancreatitis is diagnosed with blood tests and sometimes a scan, and it's usually treated in a hospital with fluids, pain control, and rest for the gut. Most mild cases settle with treatment, but severe cases can be dangerous, and early care matters. Don't try to wait it out with painkillers and fluids at home.

After an episode of alcohol-related pancreatitis, doctors generally advise stopping drinking, because further drinking raises the chance of repeat attacks and long-term damage.

### How this differs from a normal stomach ache after drinking

Plenty of people get an upset stomach after drinking. Alcohol irritates the stomach lining, and that can cause burning, nausea, and a mild ache in the upper belly. That kind of discomfort is usually milder, improves with food and time, and doesn't bore through to your back. Our [stomach pain after drinking](/never-hungover/stomach-pain-after-drinking) guide covers the more common causes. The pancreatitis pattern is more intense, more constant, and comes with vomiting that keeps going.

## Pain Under the Right Shoulder Blade: Gallbladder and Liver

The gallbladder sits under the liver on the right side of your upper belly. When a gallstone blocks its outlet, the pain often starts in the right upper belly and can spread to the right upper back or under the right shoulder blade. It tends to come on after a large, fatty meal, which is what many people eat late at night after drinking.

Gallbladder pain often lasts from about half an hour to several hours. See a doctor if you get it, and get urgent care if it comes with fever, chills, or yellowing of the skin or eyes.

The liver itself doesn't usually cause back pain. Liver problems from drinking tend to show up as tiredness, discomfort under the right ribs, swelling of the belly, or yellowing of the skin, rather than as back pain. If you've had any of those, that's a conversation for your doctor.

## Lower Back Pain After Drinking: What It Usually Means

Lower back pain is the most common version, and it's the most likely to be muscular. Ask yourself:

1. **Does it change when I move?** Pain that gets worse with bending, twisting, or getting out of bed, and eases in other positions, points to muscles or joints.
2. **Where exactly is it?** Pain across the low back, in the band of muscle just above your belt, is typical of muscles. Pain higher up and out to the side, under the ribs, is more in kidney territory.
3. **Do I feel sick in other ways?** Fever, chills, urinary symptoms, or vomiting that won't stop point away from a simple muscle ache.
4. **Is it getting better?** A muscular hangover backache should be clearly improving within a day or two.

If you have long-standing low back problems, like a disc issue or arthritis, a night out can flare them through the same routes: dehydration, bad sleep posture, and hours on your feet.

## Back Pain the Day After vs. While You're Drinking

**Back pain the next day** usually fits the muscle picture above: dehydration, sleep posture, inflammation, and a long night on your feet. It shows up when you wake and fades over the day.

**Back pain that starts while you're drinking, within minutes of a drink**, is different and less common. A few things can cause it:

- A kidney drainage problem like the UPJ narrowing described above, which hurts as fluid volume builds up.
- Acid reflux or stomach irritation felt between the shoulder blades.
- Very rarely, pain right after drinking alcohol in lymph nodes or other areas is a recognized but uncommon symptom of Hodgkin lymphoma, a type of blood cancer. This is genuinely rare, and most people with back pain while drinking don't have it. But if you get pain that reliably starts within minutes of even small amounts of alcohol, especially with swollen glands, night sweats, weight loss you can't explain, or ongoing tiredness, it's worth having a doctor take a look.

The general rule: pain that reliably and quickly follows even small amounts of alcohol is worth mentioning to a doctor, because it isn't the usual hangover pattern.

## What to Do for Back Pain After Drinking

If your pain fits the muscle picture and you don't have any of the warning signs, here's what tends to help.

### 1. Rehydrate first

Drink water steadily through the morning rather than chugging a liter at once. An oral rehydration drink or electrolyte mix helps replace sodium and potassium faster than water alone. Clear, pale urine is a reasonable sign you're catching up.

### 2. Eat something

Food helps your blood sugar recover and gives your body what it needs to repair. Foods with potassium and magnesium, like bananas, avocados, potatoes, yogurt, leafy greens, and nuts, are a good choice for tired muscles.

### 3. Move gently

It's tempting to stay in bed, but gentle movement usually helps muscle stiffness more than rest. A short walk, some easy stretches like knee-to-chest, cat-cow, or a gentle child's pose, and changing position often all help loosen tight back muscles. Stop any movement that causes sharp pain.

### 4. Use heat

A warm shower, a heating pad, or a hot water bottle on the sore area relaxes tight muscles and eases stiffness for many people. Don't fall asleep on a heating pad, and keep a layer between it and your skin.

### 5. Be careful with painkillers

Pain relievers can help, but alcohol changes the math.

- **Ibuprofen, naproxen, and aspirin (NSAIDs)** are often the go-to for muscle aches, but they irritate the stomach lining, which alcohol has already irritated, and they can strain the kidneys when you're dehydrated. If you take one, wait until you've rehydrated, take it with food, and stick to the label dose. Avoid them if you have stomach ulcers, kidney disease, or take blood thinners, and don't take them if you suspect a kidney problem. Our guide on [ibuprofen and alcohol](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol) explains the risks in detail.
- **Acetaminophen (Tylenol)** is easier on the stomach but processed by the liver. Never take it while you're still drinking or right before bed after drinking. If you drink heavily most days, ask a doctor before using it. See our [Tylenol and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) for the details.
- **Muscle relaxers and alcohol don't mix.** Many prescription muscle relaxers are sedating, and so is alcohol. Together they can slow your breathing and make you dangerously drowsy. Don't take a leftover muscle relaxer to deal with a hangover backache.

If you're not sure which painkiller is right for you, a pharmacist can tell you in a couple of minutes.

### 6. Sleep it off properly

Get a proper night's sleep in your own bed, with a pillow that keeps your neck and spine in line. If you sleep on your side, a pillow between your knees takes strain off the lower back. If you sleep on your back, a pillow under your knees helps.

## When to See a Doctor About Back Pain After Drinking

Most hangover backaches are nothing to worry about. These signs are different, and you should act on them.

**Go to the emergency room or call 911 if you have:**

- Sudden, severe pain in your back, belly, or chest
- Severe upper belly pain spreading to your back with vomiting you can't stop
- Vomiting blood, or black, tarry stools
- Confusion, fainting, or trouble staying awake
- New numbness in your groin or inner thighs, weakness in your legs, or loss of control of your bladder or bowels

**See a doctor the same day if you have:**

- Flank pain with fever, chills, or burning when you pee
- Blood in your urine, or urine that's very dark and doesn't clear up as you rehydrate
- Sharp, one-sided pain that comes in waves, especially if it moves toward your groin
- Right upper belly pain spreading to your back or shoulder blade, especially with fever or yellow skin or eyes

**Book a regular appointment if:**

- The pain lasts more than a few days or keeps coming back after you drink
- You get pain within minutes of drinking even small amounts
- You notice swollen glands, night sweats, or weight loss you can't explain
- You have back pain after most nights out, even when you drink moderately

**If you drink heavily most days,** tell your doctor. Regular heavy drinking raises the chance of pancreatitis, liver disease, and muscle damage, and a doctor can check for these with simple tests. Stopping suddenly after a long stretch of daily heavy drinking can also bring on withdrawal symptoms like shaking, sweating, anxiety, and, in serious cases, seizures. If that applies to you, cutting back with medical help is the safe way to do it.

## Can Regular Heavy Drinking Cause Ongoing Back and Muscle Pain?

For social drinkers, the answer is mostly no: occasional back pain after a night out is almost always temporary. Long-term heavy drinking is different. It can cause a condition called **alcoholic myopathy**, where muscle tissue weakens and wastes over time, often in the hips, thighs, and shoulders. Heavy drinking is also linked to lower bone density, which raises the risk of fractures later in life, and to nerve damage that can cause pain, tingling, or numbness, usually in the feet and legs first.

These problems build up over years, not weekends. If you notice muscle weakness, frequent cramps, or ongoing aches and you drink heavily, it's worth a checkup.

## How to Prevent Back Pain After Drinking

The same habits that make hangovers milder also make back pain less likely.

- **Alternate drinks with water.** A glass of water between alcoholic drinks slows your pace and limits dehydration.
- **Eat before and while you drink.** Food slows how fast alcohol is absorbed. Avoid a heavy, greasy late-night meal if you've had gallbladder trouble before.
- **Drink less, and drink slower.** The single most reliable way to avoid any hangover symptom is to drink less. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence.
- **Wear comfortable shoes** and take breaks from standing.
- **Make it to a real bed.** Couches, floors, and car seats are hard on your back, especially when alcohol stops you from shifting around.
- **Have water and electrolytes ready** for when you get home, so you can start rehydrating before bed.

### Where DHM fits in

Some people add a supplement to their routine. **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and on the liver. Most of the research is in animals and lab studies, with a small amount of human data, so it's promising, not proven. There is no good evidence that DHM prevents or treats back pain, kidney problems, or pancreatitis, and it doesn't make heavy drinking safe. What it may do, based on early research, is support how your body handles alcohol, which is why some people take it as part of a broader plan of drinking less, eating, and hydrating.

If you want to try it, popular options include [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20), a budget-friendly pure DHM tablet, and [No Days Wasted DHM Detox](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20), which adds electrolytes and other ingredients. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how much to take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. If you take prescription medication, check with your doctor or pharmacist first.

## The Bottom Line

- Most back pain after drinking is muscular: dehydration, bad sleeping positions, long hours on your feet, and hangover inflammation. It's dull, achy, changes with movement, and clears up in a day or two.
- Kidney pain is higher and more to the side, under the ribs, and doesn't change much with movement. Dehydration can cause a mild ache, but fever, burning when you pee, blood in your urine, or sharp one-sided pain need a doctor.
- Severe upper belly pain that bores through to your back, with vomiting, can be pancreatitis. Get medical care the same day.
- Water, electrolytes, food, gentle movement, and heat help most muscular backaches. Be careful with painkillers after drinking, and never mix muscle relaxers with alcohol.
- Pain that reliably starts within minutes of drinking, or keeps coming back after most nights out, is worth mentioning to a doctor.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Why does my back hurt after drinking alcohol?**

Most often it's muscular. Alcohol makes you pee more, so you lose water and electrolytes that your muscles need, and the big muscles along your spine get stiff. Add a night asleep in an awkward position, hours on your feet, and the body-wide inflammation of a hangover, and your back aches the next day. Less often, pain comes from the kidneys or pancreas, which sit near the back. Those usually come with other symptoms like fever, urinary changes, or vomiting.

**How do I know if it's kidney pain or back pain after drinking?**

Muscle pain is usually across the lower back, feels stiff or achy, and changes when you move, bend, or press on it. Kidney pain is higher and more to the side, in the flank just under the ribs, feels deeper, and doesn't change much with movement. Kidney problems also often come with urinary symptoms such as burning, cloudy or bloody urine, or fever and chills. If you have any of those, see a doctor.

**Can drinking alcohol cause upper back pain?**

Yes. Often it's muscle tension or a bad sleeping position. But severe pain in the upper middle belly that goes straight through to the upper back, especially with nausea and vomiting, can be a sign of pancreatitis. Heavy drinking is one of the two most common causes of acute pancreatitis. If your pain fits that pattern, get medical care the same day rather than waiting it out.

**Why does my lower back hurt the day after drinking?**

The most common reasons are dehydration and electrolyte loss, sleeping deeply in one awkward position because alcohol dulls the discomfort that normally makes you shift, standing or dancing for hours, and general hangover inflammation. It should improve over a day or two with water, electrolytes, food, gentle movement, and heat. If it's severe, one-sided, or comes with fever or urinary symptoms, see a doctor.

**Is it normal for your kidneys to hurt after drinking?**

A mild, dull ache in the kidney area after a night of drinking can happen with dehydration and usually fades once you rehydrate. It isn't something to ignore if it keeps happening. Sharp pain that comes in waves, pain on one side moving toward the groin, fever, chills, burning when you pee, or blood in your urine can mean a kidney stone or infection and need a doctor. Pain in the same flank every time you drink a lot of fluid can point to a drainage problem worth checking.

**What helps back pain after drinking?**

Rehydrate with water and electrolytes, eat something with potassium and magnesium, move gently instead of staying in bed, and use heat on the sore area. If you need a painkiller, wait until you've rehydrated, take it with food, and follow the label. NSAIDs like ibuprofen can be hard on the stomach and kidneys after drinking, and acetaminophen is processed by the liver. Never combine prescription muscle relaxers with alcohol.

**Can I take ibuprofen for back pain after drinking?**

Many healthy adults can take a single label dose of ibuprofen the morning after a few drinks, once they've rehydrated and eaten. But ibuprofen irritates the stomach lining, which alcohol has already irritated, and it can strain the kidneys when you're dehydrated. Avoid it if you have stomach ulcers, kidney disease, take blood thinners, or suspect your pain is coming from your kidneys. A pharmacist can help you choose.

**When should I worry about back pain after drinking?**

Get urgent care for severe upper belly pain spreading to your back with vomiting, sudden severe pain, vomiting blood, confusion, or new leg weakness, numbness in the groin, or loss of bladder or bowel control. See a doctor the same day for flank pain with fever, burning urine, or blood in your urine. Book an appointment if the pain lasts more than a few days, keeps returning after drinking, or starts within minutes of drinking even small amounts.

**Does DHM help with back pain after drinking?**

There is no good evidence that DHM prevents or treats back pain, kidney problems, or pancreatitis. DHM has been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver, mostly in animal and lab studies with limited human data. Some people use it as part of a broader approach that includes drinking less, eating, and staying hydrated, but it doesn't replace those habits or medical care.
